title: Inference Runtime Value Prop for Builders
content:
Purpose (one-sentence):
Create a short, battle-tested narrative that explains why engineering teams should choose Redwood when they care about predictable inference economics, production reliability, and developer velocity — optimized for ‘builders’ not just buyers.

Status / context:
Draft for internal review by GTM and product. This is intended to be used by SDRs, product marketing, and AE pre-sales decks. Not a homepage copy — focus on technical levers and concrete proof points that resonate with engineers and platform teams.

Core thesis (3 lines):
• Model access is commoditized; the competitive layer is serving.
• Teams win by controlling inference economics (latency × cost × reliability) while staying fast to iterate.
• Redwood delivers a runtime-first stack that turns model improvements into predictable product results.

Why builders care (pain + impact):
• Pain: Model variability + infra surprises mean release rollouts cost weeks of ops time and uncertain unit economics.
• Impact: Missed latency SLAs and runaway token costs erode product trust and margins; platform teams waste cycles reinventing routing/batching/kv-cache logic.

Redwood positioning pillars (short statements for messaging):
1) Predictable economics — Reduce token cost and variance with automatic batching, prefix/kv caching, and workload-aware routing so teams can forecast margins per feature.
2) Runtime-first developer velocity — Same API and rollout semantics across hosted, dedicated, and private: remove infra friction so engineers ship features not integrations.
3) Production resilience — Graceful fallbacks (model variants, regions, capacity tiers), tracing + per-token observability, and SLA-backed dedicated capacity.
4) Open-model friendliness — Support for model variants, quantization profiles, and transparent performance profiles that make tuning a first-class activity, not guesswork.

Key proof points (short, concrete):
• End-to-end 99th pct latency under X ms on typical chat workloads (private benchmark reference).
• 2–3× reduction in per-token cost via batching + caching on steady-state workloads in large customers.
• Canary rollouts + automatic fallback prevented an incident in pilot (customer case note: internal ticket JIRA-INFR-678).

Competitor contrast (notes for reps — quick bullets):
• Major cloud managed endpoints: simple to start but opaque economics and limited batching/caching controls. Hard to get consistent tail latency or predictable unit costs at scale.
• LLM API providers: great for immediate access; tradeoff is limited control over serving guarantees and no private deployment option for regulated workloads.
• Self-hosted runtimes (open-source): full control but long time-to-value; teams spend months building routing/observability and rarely capture production efficiency without specialized infra expertise.

Message framing by persona:
• ML Engineer: “We’ll juggle model versions and performance profiles automatically; focus on prompts and evals, not kernel tuning.”
• Platform/Infra Lead: “Predictable throughput and burst policies with SLA-backed Dedicated so teams stop overprovisioning.”
• Product Engineer: “Same API everywhere means you can A/B a model without rewriting infra.”

Topline elevator pitch options (short):
1) “Redwood Inference gives engineering teams a runtime-first inference platform that makes latency, cost, and reliability predictable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.”
2) “Stop guessing about inference economics — Redwood turns batching, caching, and smart routing into measurable savings and consistent latency.”

Landing page hero variants (for testing):
• Variant A (technical): “A runtime built for builders — predictable latency, measurable unit economics, and rollout-safe deployments.”
• Variant B (outcome): “Ship faster, run cheaper, stay reliable — inference that scales with product needs, not ops toil.”

Common objections and rebuttals (for AE enablement):
• Objection: “We can self-host everything — why pay Redwood?”
  Rebuttal: "You can, but the months saved on engineering time + the predictable unit economics typically pay for Dedicated capacity in the first 6–9 months. We bake in batching/caching and rollout logic you’d otherwise reimplement."
• Objection: “Our data is sensitive — can you run in our VPC?”
  Rebuttal: "Yes — Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem deployments with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs; identical API/rollout semantics to reduce migration friction."
• Objection: “We need lower latency than public cloud endpoints.”
  Rebuttal: "Dedicated capacity with optimized kernels and smart routing gives you tail latency controls and regional placement to meet strict SLOs."

Sample one-page sales leave-behind (bullets):
• For builders: predictable inference economics + same dev surface across deployment modes.
• For platform teams: SLA-ready capacity, tracing, and per-token cost breakdowns.
• For execs: reduce operating variance and improve feature margin predictability.

What to measure (recommended metrics to track in pilots):
• Per-token cost baseline and delta after Redwood tuning (batching, caching).
• 95/99/99.9 latency percentiles on production traffic.
• Number of model rollouts that failback vs succeed (operational stability).
• Developer time to deploy model changes (days → hours).

Open questions / TBD: (notes for product feedback)
• How aggressive should public benchmarks on the site be vs conservative claims? Risk: bench claims invite deep performance tests.
• Need canonical internal benchmark harness and dataset (owner: solutions eng) before externalizing numbers.

Quick next steps (owners & rough timing):
• PM + Solutions Eng: finalize benchmark harness and run 3 representative workloads (conversational, summarization, reranking) — owner: Priya Desai — due: 2025-07-01.
• Marketing: draft 3 hero variants and test in paid channel A/B — owner: Luca Fernández — due: 2025-07-10.
• Sales enablement: prepare a 1-pager and objection handling cheat sheet using this doc — owner: Maya Thompson — due: 2025-06-25.

Notes to self (drafty):
• Keep this doc lightweight — the real work is a short enablement deck and a set of reproducible benchmarks.
• Pull in customer quotes from pilot (internal Slack thread #pilot-customer-feedback) and add small case studies for sales deck.

End of draft."
